content_html:
An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) starts with a rate that is fixed for a set number of years and then resets at regular intervals for the rest of the loan. This calculator projects the payment through every reset, so you can see what the loan might cost after the introductory period and how high the payment could go if rates climb as fast as the loan's caps permit.

How to use this calculator

  1. Loan amount, initial rate and term: the amount you borrow, the starting rate your lender quotes and the full repayment period.
  2. Fixed-rate period: the years before the first change. A 5/1 or 5/6 ARM is fixed for 5 years; 7/1 and 10/1 loans are fixed for 7 and 10.
  3. Rate adjusts every: 12 months for a "/1" loan or 6 months for a "/6" loan.
  4. Expected rate change: how much you think the rate will move at each reset. Enter a negative value to model falling rates, or 0 to see the loan behave like a fixed-rate mortgage.
  5. Rate caps and floor: the limits written into your loan. Caps are often quoted as three numbers, such as 2/2/5: the most the first reset can move, the most each later reset can move, and the most the rate can ever rise above the starting rate.

How the payment is recalculated

During the fixed period the payment is an ordinary amortizing payment: M = B × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)−n), where B is the balance, i the monthly rate and n the number of months. At each reset the new rate is found by adding your expected change, trimmed to the cap for that reset and kept between the floor and the lifetime ceiling. The payment is then recalculated with the same formula on the remaining balance over the months left, so the loan is still paid off on schedule.

The worst-case box repeats the projection assuming the rate jumps by the full cap at every reset until it reaches the lifetime ceiling. It is not a forecast, but it is the payment your budget would need to survive.

Worked example

Take a $300,000, 30-year 5/1 ARM starting at 6% with 2/2/5 caps, and assume the rate rises 0.25% each year after the fixed period:

ItemResult
Payment for the first 5 years$1,798.65
Balance when the rate first resets$279,163.07
Payment in year 6 at 6.25%$1,841.55
Highest payment, at 11% from year 25$2,438.43
Total interest$477,497.59
Worst case: payment at 11% from year 8$2,717.83

For comparison, the same loan with no rate changes would cost $347,514.57 in interest. Because the balance shrinks over time, a rate increase late in the loan raises the payment less than the same increase early on.

Tips for evaluating an ARM

  • Ask your lender for the index, the margin and all three caps in writing. The fully indexed rate (index plus margin) shows where the rate would go today if the fixed period ended now.
  • Check the worst-case payment against your budget, not just the starting payment.
  • If you expect to sell or refinance before the first reset, the lower starting rate may matter more than later resets. Compare both loan types side by side with a fixed-vs-adjustable comparison.
  • Some ARMs have a floor equal to the margin, so the rate cannot fall below it even when the index drops.

faq.question: What do the numbers in 5/1 and 7/6 ARM mean?
faq.answer: The first number is how many years the starting rate is fixed. The second shows how often the rate can change after that: 1 means once a year and 6 means every six months.

faq.question: What is a rate cap on an adjustable-rate mortgage?
faq.answer: A cap limits how much the rate can change. Most ARMs have a cap for the first adjustment, a cap for each later adjustment and a lifetime cap on how far the rate can rise above the starting rate.

faq.question: Can my ARM payment go down?
faq.answer: Yes. If the index your loan follows falls, the rate can drop at a reset, limited by the adjustment caps and any rate floor in your loan agreement.

faq.question: Why is the expected change only an assumption?
faq.answer: Future ARM rates depend on a market index that nobody can predict. Testing a few scenarios, including the worst case, gives a better sense of risk than a single guess.

faq.question: Does this include taxes, insurance or mortgage insurance?
faq.answer: No. The results show principal and interest only. Add property tax, homeowners insurance and any mortgage insurance to estimate your full monthly housing cost.
